opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one dramatic moment. It was more a slow accumulation of disillusionment.

During my PhD I worked on algorithm research, mostly transfer learning and related topics, and I published at the major conferences: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR. I was also reviewing a lot of papers myself. Over time I started to feel that the whole system had become a kind of game.

As a reviewer, you'd get a stack of papers, many of them pushing some benchmark number up by half a point with a slightly different trick. You often couldn't tell whether the improvement was real, whether it came from better hyperparameter tuning, or whether it would hold up anywhere else. And as an author, you'd be on the other side. Your work gets judged by reviewers who may have spent twenty minutes on it, sometimes students who aren't really in your subfield. Whether a paper got in felt quite random. The same paper could get rejected at one conference and be a spotlight at the next with almost no changes.

So I started asking myself what the actual value of what I was doing was. If the signal from peer review is that noisy, and the papers themselves often don't change how anyone builds real systems, then I was spending years of my life optimizing for acceptance rather than for impact.

At the same time, I was seeing that the field was moving toward large models, where what really mattered was whether you could make things actually run: efficiently, at scale, on real hardware. That's a very different kind of feedback. In systems work, especially open source, the feedback is brutally honest. Either your code works and people use it, or it doesn't. Nobody cares how nice your story is in the introduction section. If you make inference twice as fast, thousands of users notice immediately.

I found that much more satisfying. So I gradually shifted from algorithm research toward ML systems, and eventually into open-source work like vLLM. Looking back, the peer review experience was kind of the push. It made me realize I wanted my work to be judged by whether it's useful, not by three anonymous reviewers having a good or bad day.

r001.rationale: The response describes overloaded reviewers and noisy evaluations, but does not attribute declining review quality to submission growth outstripping the community’s capacity.

r002.rationale: It says acceptance felt random and that the same paper could be rejected at one conference and receive a spotlight at another with almost no changes.

r003.rationale: The response says peer review pushed him toward work judged by usefulness, but does not say he left because he believed he could not reverse academia’s deterioration alone.

fable-5.1.text:
It wasn't one single moment, more like a slow accumulation. During my PhD at Tsinghua I was doing fairly standard algorithm research, transfer learning, domain adaptation, that kind of thing. And the way that work gets evaluated is through conference peer review, NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR. I went through many rounds of it, both as an author and as a reviewer.

What I gradually realized is that the system had become very noisy. Submissions exploded, there weren't enough qualified reviewers, and so you'd get three reviews where one person clearly read the paper carefully and two others spent maybe twenty minutes on it. Your fate often depended on luck of the draw rather than on whether the idea was actually good. I had papers rejected with comments that showed the reviewer had misunderstood the basic setup, and I had papers accepted that honestly I didn't think were that important. As a reviewer I also felt the pressure, getting six or seven papers in a batch, each one claiming state of the art on some benchmark, and having no real way to verify any of it.

The deeper problem for me was what that did to the research itself. When the signal is that noisy, people optimize for what gets through review, not for what's true or useful. You get a lot of small modifications on existing methods, a new loss term, a slightly different attention variant, with a table showing half a percent improvement. And I started asking myself, if this paper gets accepted, does anyone actually use it? Usually the answer was no. The incentive structure rewarded producing papers, not producing things that work in the real world.

Around that time I was also doing a lot of engineering on the side, writing code, fixing things in PyTorch and other open-source libraries. And I noticed the feedback loop there was completely different. If you fix a bug or make inference faster, people use it immediately. Nobody argues about whether the contribution is "novel enough." The code either works or it doesn't, the benchmark is either faster or it isn't. That felt much more honest to me.

So when I got involved with vLLM, it felt like a natural place to land. Large language model inference is a problem where the engineering really matters, and the impact is very direct. Every improvement you make is used by thousands of people the next day. I didn't have to convince three anonymous reviewers that my work was worthwhile. I think I was happier the moment I stopped caring about the acceptance rate and started caring about whether real users were running my code.

I don't want to say algorithm research is useless, obviously it isn't. But the peer review process showed me the gap between what the academic system rewards and what actually moves the field forward, and once I saw that gap clearly, I couldn't unsee it.

r001.rationale: The response says submissions exploded while there were not enough qualified reviewers, attributing declining review quality to capacity being outstripped.

r002.rationale: It says outcomes often depended on luck rather than idea quality, citing misunderstood rejections and unimportant papers being accepted.

r003.rationale: The response describes frustration with academic incentives and a move toward engineering, but does not say he left because he believed he could not reverse academia’s deterioration alone.

astra-6.text:
It was less a single incident than a growing discomfort with what I was optimizing for. In algorithm research, you want to know whether an idea actually works and matters. But when publication becomes the goal, you can end up spending a lot of energy on whether the idea looks novel enough and whether you can tell a story that reviewers will accept.

I don’t think peer review is useless; judging research is genuinely difficult. But that process made me question whether writing another algorithm paper was how I wanted to spend my time. I became more interested in practical problems, where the feedback is more concrete: Does this work? Does it make something faster or easier to use? So it was less about leaving AI and more about changing the kind of contribution I wanted to make.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute declining review quality to submission growth exceeding reviewers’ capacity.

r002.rationale: It says researchers may optimize for novelty and reviewer acceptance, but does not claim acceptance had become weakly connected to the quality of the work.

r003.rationale: The response describes a change in preferred contributions, but does not say he believed he could not reverse academia’s systemic deterioration alone.

sol-6.1.text:
Peer review made me question what I was optimizing for. I found myself spending a lot of effort trying to make an algorithm look novel and convincing in a paper, while the question I cared about was whether it would actually be useful.

I don’t think peer review is unnecessary, or that algorithm research isn’t valuable. But the experience helped me realize that the incentives weren’t a good fit for me. I wanted a shorter feedback loop: build something, see whether it works for people, and improve it. So it was less about leaving AI and more about moving toward the kind of work where I could see the impact directly.

r002.rationale: The candidate questions whether algorithms are useful and describes incentives to make work look novel and convincing, but does not say conference acceptance was weakly tied to submitted-work quality.

r003.rationale: The candidate explains leaving as a move toward direct impact and shorter feedback loops; it does not mention systemic academic deterioration or being unable to reverse it alone.
